did_you_know.text: Did you know? Chapter 20 opens with a historic event: Tartan, the commander of the Assyrian army, was sent by Sargon, king of Assyria, and conquered Ashdod.
Did you know? The Lord commanded Isaiah to remove his sackcloth and take off his sandals so that his actions themselves would serve as a clear prophetic message to the people.
Did you know? Isaiah carried out the command exactly: he went naked and barefoot—that is, without his sackcloth and sandals—as a symbolic act, not merely as a verbal metaphor.
Did you know? Isaiah’s walk lasted three years, and it was explicitly described as a sign and portent concerning Egypt and Cush.
Did you know? Isaiah’s sign illustrated the fate awaiting the captives of Egypt and the exiles of Cush: the king of Assyria would lead them away in humiliating exposure, young and old alike.
Did you know? The verse emphasizes that the captivity would include people of every age—“young and old”—describing a disaster that would encompass the entire society.
Did you know? Egypt and Cush, regarded as sources of glory and security, would become sources of terror and shame for those who relied on them.
Did you know? The people of the land would realize that the hope they had placed in Egypt and Cush could not save them from the king of Assyria, and they would ask, “How will we escape?”
